{{short description|Geometric property of objects being in the same plane}}

In [[geometry]], a set of points in space are '''coplanar''' if there exists a geometric [[Plane (mathematics)|plane]] that contains them all. For example, three points are always coplanar, and if the points are distinct and [[non-collinear points|non-collinear]], the plane they determine is unique. However, a set of four or more distinct points will, in general, not lie in a single plane.
[[File:Coplanar points.svg|thumb|An example of coplanar points]]
Two [[Line (geometry)|lines]] in three-dimensional space are coplanar if there is a plane that includes them both. This occurs if the lines are [[Parallel (geometry)|parallel]], or if they [[Line-line intersection|intersect]] each other. Two lines that are not coplanar are called [[skew lines]].

[[Distance geometry]] provides a solution technique for the problem of determining whether a set of points is coplanar, knowing only the distances between them.

==Properties in three dimensions==
In three-dimensional space, two [[linearly independent]] vectors with the same initial point determine a plane through that point. Their [[cross product]] is a [[normal (geometry)|normal]] vector to that plane, and any vector [[orthogonal]] to this cross product through the initial point will lie in the plane.<ref>{{citation|first=Earl W.|last=Swokowski|title=Calculus with Analytic Geometry|edition=Alternate|year=1983|publisher=Prindle, Weber & Schmidt|isbn=0-87150-341-7|page=[https://archive.org/details/calculuswithanal00swok/page/647 647]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/calculuswithanal00swok/page/647}}</ref> This leads to the following coplanarity test using a [[scalar triple product]]:

Four distinct points, {{math|''x''{{sub|1}}, ''x''{{sub|2}}, ''x''{{sub|3}}, ''x''{{sub|4}}}}, are coplanar if and only if,
:<math>[(x_2 - x_1) \times (x_4 - x_1)] \cdot (x_3 - x_1) = 0.</math>
which is also equivalent to
:<math>(x_2 - x_1) \cdot [(x_4 - x_1) \times (x_3 - x_1)] = 0.</math>
 
If three vectors {{math|'''a''', '''b''', '''c'''}} are coplanar, then if {{math|1='''a''' ⋅ '''b''' = 0}} (i.e., {{math|'''a'''}} and {{math|'''b'''}} are orthogonal) then
:<math>(\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{\hat a})\mathbf{\hat a} + (\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{\hat b})\mathbf{\hat b}  = \mathbf{c}, </math>

where {{tmath|\mathbf \hat a}} denotes the [[unit vector]] in the [[direction (geometry)|direction]] of {{math|'''a'''}}. That is, the [[vector projection]]s of {{math|'''c'''}} on {{math|'''a'''}} and {{math|'''c'''}} on {{math|'''b'''}} add to give the original {{math|'''c'''}}.
<!--
===Plane formula===
Another technique involves computing the formula for the planes defined by each subset of three non-[[collinear]] points. First, the [[normal vector]] for each plane is computed using some [[orthogonalization]] technique. If the planes are parallel, then the dot-product of their unit normal vectors will be 1 or −1. More specifically, the angle between the normal vectors can be computed. This is called the dihedral angle, and represents the smallest possible angle between the two planes. The formula for a plane in 3-dimensional space is:

:<math>ax+by+cz+d=0,</math> where {{math|(''a, b, c'')}} is the normal vector of the plane.

The value {{mvar|d}} can be computed by substituting one of the points and then solving. If {{mvar|d}} is the same for all subsets of three points, then the planes are the same.

One advantage of this technique is that it can work in higher dimensional spaces. For example, suppose one wants to compute the dihedral angle between two {{mvar|m}}-dimensional hyperplanes defined by {{mvar|m}} points in ({{math|''m'' + 1}})-dimensional space. If {{math|''n – m'' > 1}}, then there are an infinite number of normal vectors for each hyperplane, so the angle between two of them is not necessarily the dihedral angle. However, if the [[Gram–Schmidt process]] is used, using the same initial vector in both cases, then the angle between the two normal vectors will be minimal, and therefore will be the dihedral angle between the hyperplanes.
-->

==Coplanarity of points in ''n'' dimensions whose coordinates are given==

Since three or fewer points are always coplanar, the problem of determining when a set of points is coplanar is generally of interest only when there are at least four points involved. In the case that there are exactly four points, several ''ad hoc'' methods can be employed, but a general method that works for any number of points uses vector methods and the property that a plane is determined by two [[linearly independent vectors]].

In an {{mvar|n}}-dimensional space where {{math|''n'' ≥ 3}}, a set of {{mvar|k}} points <math>\{p_0,\ p_1,\ \dots,\ p_{k-1}\}</math> are coplanar if and only if the matrix of their relative differences, that is, the matrix whose columns (or rows) are the vectors <math display=”inline”>\overrightarrow{p_0 p_1},\ \overrightarrow{p_0 p_2},\ \dots,\  \overrightarrow{p_0 p_{k-1}} </math> is of [[rank (linear algebra)|rank]] 2 or less. 

For example, given four points
:<math>\begin{align}
X &= (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n), \\
Y &= (y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n), \\
Z &= (z_1, z_2, \dots, z_n), \\
W &= (w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n), 
\end{align}</math>
if the [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]]
:<math>\begin{bmatrix}
x_1 - w_1 & x_2 - w_2 & \dots & x_n - w_n \\
y_1 - w_1 & y_2 - w_2 & \dots & y_n - w_n \\
z_1 - w_1 & z_2 - w_2 & \dots & z_n - w_n \\
\end{bmatrix}</math>
is of rank 2 or less, the four points are coplanar.

In the special case of a plane that contains the origin, the property can be simplified in the following way:
A set of {{mvar|k}} points and the origin are coplanar if and only if the matrix of the coordinates of the {{mvar|k}} points is of rank 2 or less.

==Geometric shapes==

A [[skew polygon]] is a [[polygon]] whose [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]] are not coplanar. Such a polygon must have at least four vertices; there are no skew triangles.

A [[polyhedron]] that has positive [[volume]] has vertices that are not all coplanar.
